newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: SOCCER-DOCTOR SAYS MARADONA WON'T DROP DEAD FROM DRUGS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-DOCTOR SAYS MARADONA WON'T DROP DEAD FROM DRUGS.

text.p: Boca Juniors' team doctor cast doubt on a magazine story that former Argentina soccer captain Diego Maradona has burnt out his brain's frontal lobes by cocaine sniffing and is in danger of dropping dead.
Dr Homero De Agostino told the Ole sport daily Wednesday he doubted that brain scans showed irreparable damage to the 35-year-old midfielder, who has publicly admitted a drug habit.

"I don't think that it is really like that. I never asked for Maradona to undergo a study of that sort, a nuclear magnetic resonance test, because it did not seem to me that there was any justification for doing it."
Dr de Agostino's comments contrast with those of Dr Ricardo Grimson who said: "I have not ruled out the fear that Diego could suddenly die on a football pitch or walking down the street."
Dr de Agostino dismissed claims in the Noticias news weekly that Maradona's years of abuse had so physically weakened him that he could collapse and die during a match.

Noticias printed the headline "Maradona's dead zone" superimposed over a picture of a brain scan -- without saying whose it was -- on its front cover Sunday. They juxtaposed it with a photo of the star with a vacant expression on his face.

Claiming to have had access to a brain scan carried out last year as well as to subsequent medical tests, Noticias wrote: "The diagnosis is final: "Cell death in the frontal lobe with loss of blood circulation.' He cannot control his aggression, or detect people standing behind him."
According to the magazine, "Maradona is in the final stage of progressive irreparable damage."
Argentina's 1986 World Cup champion has yet to reply with legal action to the story, which followed another round of outrageous behavior by the star.
After a highly-publicized trip to Switzerland for drug rehabilitation treatment in August, he suffered an attack of fury in a Spanish hotel where he smashed furniture after getting stuck in a lift.

Maradona is also at the center of accusations by a Buenos Aires weightlifter, Sergio Parodi, that his urine sample was switched with another player's in a post-match drugs test last August. The other player was then announced to have tested positive for cocaine.

But Boca Juniors coach Carlos Bilardo defended Maradona, who played for his team last season but has yet to decide whether he will do so again. Accusing Parodi of trying to take advantage of Maradona's fame, he said, "Diego's test result was negative and that's that."
Maradona says he is going to sue Bilardo, along with other former colleagues and acquaintances, for comments he made to British journalist Jimmy Burns in his unauthorized biography "The Hand of God".
Once the most expensive player in the world, Maradona's career has since been dogged by scandal.
In 1994 he was banned from international matches for 15 months after failing a dope test at the World Cup finals in the United States.
In a stressful moment a few months earlier he had fired at reporters with an air rifle.
In 1991 he was also banned for 15 months for testing positive for cocaine while playing for Napoli.
